# How Light Is an Electron?

## A Glowing Spot

Nobody has ever seen a single electron, and no balance can weigh one. What Thomson could see was a glowing spot where the rays hit the end of the tube. When the charged plates were switched on, the spot moved, and he could measure how far it moved.

<!-- STEP id="lighter" -->
## Lighter Particles Bend More

A gust of wind pushes a paper ball a long way, but it hardly moves a cricket ball. In the same way, the same electric push bends a light particle much more than a heavy one. So how far the spot moves tells us how light the particles are.

Try it: compare an electron with a charged hydrogen atom under the same push.

<!-- STEP id="number" -->
## About 1/1836 of a Hydrogen Atom

Hydrogen is the lightest atom, and even a charged hydrogen atom hardly bends at all. From such measurements we know that an electron has about **1/1836** of the mass of a hydrogen atom. In 1909, Robert Millikan measured the charge of an electron, which is now taken as -1, and this made the value of the mass exact.

**You would need about 1836 electrons to match the mass of one hydrogen atom.**
